complexity.low: One area. The behavior is already decided. A focused change and tests.
complexity.medium: Two or three compiler phases, or a semantic choice that can break programs.
complexity.high: The type model, the C ABI, or ownership. Easy to get wrong.

outOfScope: Structs, tuples, maps, and error values
Directory packages and one C file per module
HTTP on Windows, and HTTP together with GPU
Type inference, generics, methods, interfaces, pointers, nil, defer, and goroutines
Lexer extras: block comments, raw strings, hex literals, underscores in numbers, scientific notation
Treating an infinite for whose body returns as a terminating function
Panicking in code generation on states the type checker already rejected
A math package, command-line args, environment variables, and formatted printing

tickets.title: Align the language docs with the compiler
tickets.whatToBuild: The spec, module docs, README, and GPU notes match the compiler a user can run today. Nested collections and pub are documented as present. The standard packages include image, time, http, and gpu. The pipeline includes CUDA. Integer division traps and float division follows IEEE. The old review transcript is marked historical.
acceptanceCriteria: The spec describes nested list, slice, and array element types as supported.
The spec describes pub and package-qualified calls as implemented.
The module docs list image, time, http, and gpu as bare imports.
The README pipeline includes CUDA and nvcc for programs that declare a kernel.
The spec states that integer division by zero and signed integer overflow trap, and that float division follows IEEE.
The GPU notes state that device arithmetic traps without a Trux error message.
The old review transcript is marked historical, and the fixed return-path, name-mangling, integer-arithmetic, evaluation-order, and -O2 items are not listed as open work.

tickets.title: Tighten for headers and parameter lists
tickets.whatToBuild: The three for forms parse as three productions, and a parameter list may end with a comma. Existing programs keep their current behavior.
acceptanceCriteria: for {}, for condition {}, and for init; condition; post {} each parse as that form.
A for post statement still cannot be let.
An if immediately after a block on the same line is still rejected.
A trailing comma in a parameter list is accepted.
Expression lists still accept a trailing comma.
Existing examples and the compiler test suite still parse and run.

tickets.title: Add prefix minus and boolean not
tickets.whatToBuild: Users can negate a number and negate a boolean. Both forms compile, format, highlight, and run in ordinary functions and in kernels. Negating the minimum int fails as an integer overflow.
acceptanceCriteria: -1 and -x compile and run for int and for float.
!flag and !(a == b) compile and run.
Negating the minimum int fails as an integer overflow on the host.
Kernels accept prefix minus and boolean not.
trux fmt and editor highlighting cover both prefixes.
Existing programs still compile and run.

tickets.title: Add remainder
tickets.whatToBuild: Users can write a % b for ints. A zero divisor fails. The minimum int remainder -1 fails as overflow. Host functions and kernels share that behavior. Precedence matches multiplication and division.
acceptanceCriteria: a % b compiles and runs for int operands and yields the remainder.
A zero divisor fails as a Trux runtime error on the host.
The minimum int remainder -1 fails as overflow on the host.
Kernels accept % and trap on a zero divisor and on that overflow case.
a % b * c groups as (a % b) * c.
trux fmt and editor highlighting cover %.
Float remainder is rejected.

tickets.title: Add short-circuit && and ||
tickets.whatToBuild: Users can combine boolean conditions with && and ||. The right operand is skipped when the left operand decides the result. A side-effecting read on the skipped side does not run. Kernels accept the same operators. Precedence is below comparisons, and && binds tighter than ||.
acceptanceCriteria: a && b is true only when both operands are true, and a || b is true when either operand is true.
io.readInt() on the right of && is not consumed when the left operand is false.
io.readInt() on the right of || is not consumed when the left operand is true.
a == b && c == d parses with the comparisons inside the &&.
a && b || c parses as (a && b) || c.
Kernels accept && and ||.
trux fmt and editor highlighting cover both operators.
Non-bool operands are rejected.

tickets.title: Add break and continue
tickets.whatToBuild: break leaves the innermost loop. continue runs that loop's post statement once, then starts the next iteration. Nested loops obey the innermost loop. Host functions and kernels behave the same way. A for condition with a side effect still evaluates once per iteration when the body continues.
acceptanceCriteria: break leaves the innermost loop and does not run its post statement.
continue runs the innermost loop's post statement once, then evaluates the condition for the next iteration.
In nested loops, break and continue affect only the innermost loop.
A side-effecting for condition runs once per iteration, including an iteration entered through continue.
Host functions and kernels accept both statements.
break and continue outside a loop are rejected.
trux fmt and editor highlighting cover both statements.

tickets.title: Simplify generated function signatures
tickets.whatToBuild: Existing programs still compile and run. Ordinary functions void-cast the context and result-arena parameters without a usage tracker. A kernel prototype and its definition are written by one signature path. The language a user writes does not change.
acceptanceCriteria: The compiler test suite passes.
Generated ordinary functions still compile and run when the context or the result arena is unused.
Generated code no longer tracks whether those parameters were used.
A kernel prototype and its definition stay in agreement and come from one signature path.
Existing kernel programs still compile.

tickets.title: Record nested collection families while building IR
tickets.whatToBuild: A program that uses nested lists or slices still emits the runtime types it needs. Those types are collected while the IR is built, so a new IR form does not need a second walk of the finished IR.
acceptanceCriteria: A program that uses list[list[int]] and [][]T still compiles, runs, and clones nested values.
The runtime collection types for those programs are recorded during IR build.
Code generation no longer walks the finished IR only to discover nested collection families.
The compiler test suite passes.

tickets.title: Type-check library files and tests in the language server
tickets.whatToBuild: Opening a file with no main, or a .test.tx file, reports type errors in the editor. A legal test function is not flagged for a missing return type. Files that already have a main still report type errors.
acceptanceCriteria: A library file with no main reports a type error for an undefined name, a bad call, or a mismatched let.
A .test.tx file reports a type error in a test function.
A legal test function, with no parameters and no declared return type, is not reported as missing a return type.
A file with main still reports type errors.
Parse errors are still reported for every file.

tickets.title: Pool frame-arena chunks
tickets.whatToBuild: A hot function that allocates on each call reuses frame chunks instead of allocating and freeing one every call. Recursive calls still get their own chunks. Program results do not change.
acceptanceCriteria: A function that allocates a small string or slice on every call reuses a frame chunk across calls after the first.
Recursive calls and nested calls still return correct owned and borrowed values.
The chunk pool lives with the runtime context, so two contexts do not share chunks.
Existing ownership examples and the compiler test suite still pass.
A small benchmark shows less allocator traffic than a build that frees the frame chunk on every return.

tickets.title: Elide frame arenas that do not allocate
tickets.whatToBuild: A function that only returns scalars or borrowed views no longer creates and destroys a frame arena. A function that allocates still creates one. Borrowed returns and owned returns stay valid.
acceptanceCriteria: Generated code for a function that returns only an int, a bool, a float, or a borrowed parameter view does not create a frame arena.
A function that allocates a string, a slice, a list, or an owned return still creates a frame arena and cleans it up.
Borrowed slice returns and cloned owned returns still outlive the callee.
Existing ownership examples and the compiler test suite still pass.

tickets.title: Cut avoidable runtime allocations
tickets.whatToBuild: List creation registers less heap traffic, io.readFile reads the file in one buffer, and a large frame grows chunks geometrically. Each change keeps current program results and is checked with its own benchmark.
acceptanceCriteria: Creating a list still appends, indexes, and clones with the same results, and the list header is not a separate heap allocation from its registration.
io.readFile returns the same file contents and reads the file into one buffer.
A frame that needs more than one chunk grows later chunks geometrically.
Each of the three changes has a benchmark recorded before it is kept.
The chunk pool from the blocking ticket still reuses frame chunks.
Existing IO, collection, and ownership examples still pass.

tickets.title: Rewind non-escaping loop temporaries
tickets.whatToBuild: A loop whose temporary strings or slices die at the end of the iteration reuses that frame memory on the next iteration. A value stored past the iteration, appended to a list, or returned is kept. Recursion and nested calls stay valid.
acceptanceCriteria: A loop that builds a temporary string or slice and does not store it outside the iteration reuses the frame memory on the next iteration.
A loop value assigned to a variable declared outside the loop, appended to a list, or returned is still valid after the iteration and after the function returns.
Nested calls and recursive calls that allocate inside the loop stay valid.
A stress program covers both the escaping case and the non-escaping case.
The chunk pool from the blocking ticket still reuses frame chunks.
Existing ownership examples still pass.
